summary: Describes using AES in Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM) mode, with an explicit initialization vector, in IPsec ESP to provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, and connectionless integrity. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: IPsec protects packets with an algorithm pair chosen when the connection is set up. This RFC adds one such choice: the Advanced Encryption Standard used in CCM mode, a method that encrypts and checks the integrity of a packet in one pass, with the per-packet nonce carried in the packet itself. It spells out exactly where the nonce, the ciphertext and the integrity check go in an ESP packet.

subtitle: How the Advanced Encryption Standard in CCM mode protects an IPsec ESP packet, with the nonce in the packet.

tldr.problem: IPsec needs a transform that encrypts a packet, shows that it came from the claimed sender and detects any change in transit. AES is a block cipher and needs a mode of operation before it can be used that way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes AES in CCM mode, which encrypts with counter mode and checks integrity with CBC-MAC in one pass, and places the pieces in an ESP packet: an 8-octet initialization vector in front, the ciphertext, then the integrity check value.
tldr.outcome: IANA assigned three ESP transform identifiers for it, 14, 15 and 16, for the three permitted check value sizes. The RFC insists on fresh keys, because reusing a counter value with the same key leaks the XOR of two plaintexts.

today: RFC 4309 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification for using AES in CCM mode with an explicit IV as an IPsec ESP transform.

sections.title: What This RFC Adds to IPsec
sections.content:
The Advanced Encryption Standard is a block cipher, and it can be used in many different modes. This document describes the use of AES in CCM (Counter with CBC-MAC) mode, with an explicit initialization vector, as an IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload mechanism to provide confidentiality, data origin authentication and connectionless integrity.

The document does not provide an overview of IPsec. Information about how the various components of IPsec work together to provide security services is available in RFC 4301 and RFC 2411.
sections.plainLanguage: AES is a block cipher, and it can be used in many different modes. This RFC describes AES in CCM mode with an explicit initialization vector, used as an IPsec transform that gives confidentiality, checks that the data came from the claimed sender, and protects it against change in transit.

sections.title: How CCM Mode Works
sections.content:
CCM is a generic authenticate-and-encrypt block cipher mode, and in this specification it is used with the AES block cipher. AES CCM has two parameters.

M indicates the size of the integrity check value. CCM defines values of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16 octets, but to maintain alignment and provide adequate security only the values that are a multiple of four and are at least eight are permitted. Implementations MUST support M values of 8 octets and 16 octets, and MAY support an M value of 12 octets. L indicates the size of the length field in octets; CCM defines values between 2 and 8, and this specification supports only L = 4, which accommodates a full Jumbogram. The length includes all of the encrypted data, which also includes the ESP Padding, Pad Length and Next Header fields.

There are four inputs to CCM originator processing. The key is a single key used both to calculate the integrity check value with CBC-MAC and to perform payload encryption using counter mode; AES supports key sizes of 128, 192 and 256 bits, and implementations MUST support 128 bits. The nonce is 15-L octets, so 11 octets here, and implementations MUST support a nonce of 11 octets. The payload is the payload of the ESP packet, which MUST NOT be longer than 4,294,967,295 octets, the maximum size of a Jumbogram, including the ESP Padding, Pad Length and Next Header fields. The AAD, additional authenticated data, covers data outside the payload: CCM does not allow AAD longer than 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 octets, and the integrity check value is computed from the ESP header, payload and trailer fields, which is far smaller than that limit.
sections.plainLanguage: CCM combines two steps. It encrypts with counter mode, and it computes a message authentication code with CBC-MAC over the same data. One key is used for both. Two parameters control it: M is the length of the integrity check, and only 8, 12 and 16 octets are allowed, of which 8 and 16 must be supported. L is the length of the length field, and this RFC supports only the value 4.

sections.title: Where the Pieces Go in the ESP Packet
sections.content:
The ESP payload is composed of the IV followed by the ciphertext, with the authentication data after it. The initialization vector field MUST be eight octets. The IV MUST be chosen by the encryptor in a manner that ensures that the same IV value is used only once for a given key, and the encryptor can generate it in any manner that ensures uniqueness; common approaches include incrementing a counter for each packet and linear feedback shift registers.

Including the IV in each packet ensures that the decryptor can generate the key stream needed for decryption, even when some datagrams are lost or reordered.

The encrypted payload contains the ciphertext. AES CCM mode does not require plaintext padding, but ESP does require padding to 32-bit word-align the authentication data. The Padding, Pad Length and Next Header fields MUST be concatenated with the plaintext before performing encryption, and the padding MUST be generated and checked in accordance with the conventions in RFC 4303.

AES CCM provides an encrypted integrity check value, and the one it provides is carried in the Authentication Data fields without further encryption. Implementations MUST support ICV sizes of 8 octets and 16 octets and MAY support an ICV of 12 octets.

The initialization vector and the integrity check value are the only sources of packet expansion. The IV always adds 8 octets to the front of the payload, and the ICV is added at the end of the payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The ESP payload holds three things in order. First an 8-octet initialization vector, then the encrypted payload, then the authentication data, which is the integrity check value. The IV is added in front of every packet and the check value at the end, and those two are the only additions to the packet size.

sections.title: The Nonce and the Counter Block
sections.content:
Each packet conveys the IV that is necessary to construct the sequence of counter blocks used by counter mode to generate the key stream. The AES counter block is 16 octets. One octet is used for the CCM Flags, and 4 octets are used for the block counter, as specified by the CCM L parameter. The remaining octets are the nonce, which occupies the second through the twelfth octets in the counter block.

The salt field is 24 bits and contains an unpredictable value. It MUST be assigned at the beginning of the security association. The salt value need not be secret, but it MUST NOT be predictable prior to the beginning of the security association. The initialization vector field is 64 bits and, as described earlier, must be chosen so that the same value is used only once for a given key.

This construction permits each packet to consist of up to 2^32 blocks, which is 4,294,967,296 blocks or 68,719,476,736 octets. It therefore provides more key stream for each packet than is needed to handle any IPv6 Jumbogram.
sections.plainLanguage: The nonce that drives the counter mode is built from two parts: a 24-bit salt chosen when the security association starts, and the 64-bit IV from the packet. Together they are 11 octets, which sit in the 16-octet counter block along with one octet of flags and a four-octet block counter. The salt does not have to be secret, but it must not be predictable before the association starts.

sections.title: Protecting the Headers as Well
sections.content:
The data integrity and data origin authentication for the Security Parameters Index and the (Extended) Sequence Number fields is provided without encrypting them. Two formats are defined: one for 32-bit sequence numbers and one for 64-bit extended sequence numbers. In both, the SPI is followed by the sequence number.

Sequence Numbers are conveyed in canonical network byte order. Extended Sequence Numbers are conveyed in canonical network byte order, placing the high-order 32 bits first and the low-order 32 bits second. Canonical network byte order is fully described in RFC 791, Appendix B.
sections.plainLanguage: The SPI and the sequence number are not encrypted, but they are covered by the integrity check. The RFC defines two formats: the SPI followed by a 32-bit sequence number, or the SPI followed by a 64-bit extended sequence number. A reader can check the integrity of these fields without decrypting anything.

sections.title: How IKE Supplies the Key and the Salt
sections.content:
This section describes the conventions used to generate keying material and salt values for AES CCM using the Internet Key Exchange protocol. Implementations MUST use fresh keys with AES CCM, and IKE can be used to establish them.

IKE makes use of a pseudo-random function to derive keying material of arbitrary size, called KEYMAT, and keying material is extracted from the output string without regard to boundaries. The size of KEYMAT MUST be three octets longer than is needed for the associated AES key. For AES CCM with a 128-bit key, the KEYMAT requested is 19 octets: the first 16 octets are the AES key and the remaining three are used as the salt value in the counter block. For a 192-bit key it is 27 octets, the first 24 being the key and the last three the salt. For a 256-bit key it is 35 octets, the first 32 being the key and the last three the salt. This convention provides a salt value that is secret as well as unpredictable.

For IKE Phase 2 negotiations, IANA has assigned three ESP Transform Identifiers for AES CCM with an explicit IV: 14 for AES CCM with an 8-octet ICV, 15 for a 12-octet ICV and 16 for a 16-octet ICV. Because AES supports three key lengths, the Key Length attribute MUST be specified in the IKE Phase 2 exchange, and it MUST have a value of 128, 192 or 256. This document does not specify conventions for using AES CCM in IKE Phase 1 negotiations, because a separate specification and an Encryption Algorithm Identifier would be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: IKE can supply the key and the salt. The keying material is three octets longer than the AES key: 19 octets for a 128-bit key, 27 for 192 bits and 35 for 256. The last three octets become the salt. Three ESP transform identifiers are registered for IKE phase 2: 14 for an 8-octet check value, 15 for 12 octets and 16 for 16 octets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
AES CCM employs counter mode for confidentiality. If a counter value is ever used for more than one packet with the same key, the same key stream is used to encrypt both packets and the confidentiality guarantees are voided.

The RFC shows why. If the encryptor XORs the same key stream with two different packet plaintexts, and both ciphertext streams are exposed to an attacker, then the ciphertexts XORed together give the two plaintexts XORed together, which is relatively straightforward to separate. Thus, using any stream cipher, including AES CTR, to encrypt two plaintexts under the same key stream leaks the plaintext.

AES CCM should therefore not be used with statically configured keys, because extraordinary measures would be needed to prevent the reuse of a counter block value with the static key across power cycles. To be safe, implementations MUST use fresh keys with AES CCM, and IKE or IKEv2 can be used to establish them.

When IKE is used to establish fresh keys between two peers, separate keys are established for the two traffic flows. If a different mechanism establishes only a single key, there is a high probability that the peers will select the same IV values for some packets, so ESP implementations that permit the same key for both directions with the same peer MUST ensure that the two peers assign different salt values to the security association.

Regardless of the mode used, AES with a 128-bit key is vulnerable to the birthday attack after 2^64 blocks are encrypted with a single key. Since ESP with Extended Sequence Numbers allows for up to 2^64 packets in a single security association, there is real potential for more than 2^64 blocks to be encrypted with one key. Implementations SHOULD generate a fresh key before 2^64 blocks are encrypted with the same key, or SHOULD make use of the longer AES key sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: Reusing a counter value with the same key is catastrophic, because the same key stream encrypts two packets and an attacker who sees both ciphertexts can recover the XOR of the two plaintexts. The RFC therefore requires fresh keys for AES CCM and states that static keys are inappropriate. It also notes that a 128-bit key is vulnerable to a birthday attack after 2^64 blocks, so implementations should rekey before that or use a longer key.

sections.title: Why an Explicit IV
sections.content:
In the development of this specification, the use of the ESP sequence number field instead of an explicit IV field was considered, and this section documents the rationale for the selection of an explicit IV. The choice is not a cryptographic security issue, as either approach prevents counter block collisions.

The use of an explicit IV does not dictate the manner that the encryptor uses to assign the per-packet value in the counter block. Only the encryptor can ensure that the value is not used for more than one packet, so there is no advantage to a mechanism that lets the decryptor determine whether counter block values collide: the damage from a collision is done whether or not the decryptor detects it. The explicit IV allows adders, linear feedback shift registers, and any other technique that meets the encryptor's time budget, so long as it results in a unique value for each packet. Adders are simple but, due to carries, they do not execute in constant time, while LFSRs offer an alternative that does. The assignment of the per-packet counter block value needs to be inside the assurance boundary, since some implementations assign the sequence number inside that boundary and others do not, and a sequence number collision does not have the dire consequences of a counter block collision.

The additional overhead of 64 bits for the IV field is acceptable. As normally employed, CBC requires a full block for the IV and, on average, half a block for padding, so AES CCM confidentiality processing with an explicit IV has about one third of the overhead of AES CBC, and the overhead is constant for each packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC considered using the ESP sequence number as the IV and explains why it chose an explicit IV field instead. Only the sender can guarantee that a value is never reused, and a counter block collision does damage whether or not the receiver notices it. An explicit IV lets the sender use any method that produces a unique value, including a simple counter or a shift register, and it costs 64 bits per packet, about a third of the overhead of CBC mode.

fields.name: Initialization Vector
fields.desc: Eight octets. The encryptor chooses it so that the same value is used only once for a given key.

fields.name: Encrypted Payload
fields.desc: The ciphertext, including the ESP Padding, Pad Length and Next Header fields.

fields.name: Authentication Data
fields.desc: The integrity check value from CCM, carried without further encryption. Its size is set by the M parameter.

viz.caption: THE NONCE AS IT SITS IN THE 16-OCTET COUNTER BLOCK

fields.name: Block Counter
fields.desc: Four octets, the size set by the L parameter.

fields.name: Salt
fields.desc: An unpredictable value assigned at the start of the security association. It need not be secret.

fields.name: Initialization Vector
fields.desc: The 64-bit IV carried in the packet, used only once for a given key.

items.title: Key
items.text: One key for both CBC-MAC and counter mode. 128 bits must be supported, 192 and 256 may be.

items.title: Nonce
items.text: 11 octets, built from a 24-bit salt and the 64-bit IV of the packet.

items.title: Payload
items.text: The ESP payload, up to 4,294,967,295 octets including the trailer fields.

items.title: AAD
items.text: Data outside the payload that the integrity check covers, here the ESP header, payload and trailer.
